tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to see the product from a user's perspective: a project timesheet for logging work, leave, reminders, reporting, and administration. It also frames the key architectural choice that shapes the rest of the tour: one application can use Supabase or native PostgreSQL, alongside companion mobile apps.

tour.title: Web Application Shell
tour.description: The browser experience begins at the sign-in page, where credential validation and the client authentication flow bring a user into the system. The root layout wraps that page and the rest of the app with server-derived branding, global styles, and notifications, establishing the shared frame for every route.
tour.languageLesson: In React, a root layout provides a persistent component boundary around route content; page components supply the content for an individual route.

tour.title: Shared Data Contracts
tour.description: Building on the web shell, shared TypeScript types define the vocabulary used by UI, API contracts, domain features, and persistence. The repository contract then gives both database adapters the same operations, while the database facade selects the configured implementation and keeps callers backend-neutral.
tour.languageLesson: A TypeScript interface or type can act as a contract between independent implementations, allowing callers to depend on behavior and data shape rather than a specific database client.

tour.title: Authentication Adapters
tour.description: The same interchangeable design applies to identity: an authentication facade exposes stable session and actor lookups while delegating to the native or Supabase adapter. Native mode verifies credentials and issues signed-cookie sessions; Supabase mode retrieves the user and actor through its RLS-aware client.

tour.title: Timesheet Workflows
tour.description: With the shared types and backend boundary in place, Server Actions implement the actual work users and project managers perform. Timesheet actions validate entries, enforce authorization and rate limits, and persist single or batch changes; project actions apply role checks before validating and saving project updates.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js Server Actions let UI code request server-side mutations through a typed function boundary; authorization and validation still belong on the server because client-side checks alone cannot protect data.

tour.title: Database Evolution
tour.description: These migration nodes show how the shared repository contract is backed by two evolving schemas. The native initial migration creates core profile, project, timesheet, leave, reminder, and settings tables, while the Supabase initial migration defines core tables together with authentication helpers and row-level security policies.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations record incremental schema changes so each deployment can move a database forward in a known order; row-level security policies add database-enforced access rules in Supabase.

tour.title: Mobile Application
tour.description: The mobile app reuses a shared React Native shell for workspace setup, authenticated navigation, session state, theming, offline status, and recovery. Its HTTP client connects the experience to the service, while Android, iOS, and Windows each provide a native host that boots the shared JavaScript application.
tour.languageLesson: React Native shares most screens and business logic across platforms, while native host code handles platform-specific startup and integrations.

tour.title: Verification Across Layers
tour.description: The tests connect the architecture back to observable behavior: action tests cover timesheet rules and rejected or security-sensitive operations, while separate data-client tests exercise both backend modes. The mobile app also has its own startup tests, so verification spans the browser mutation path, backend boundary, and companion client.

tour.title: Container Deployment
tour.description: The deployment guide explains how the native build runs on OpenShift or Kubernetes and contrasts that route with the Supabase and Vercel option introduced at the start. The Dockerfile and Compose definition package and run the application locally or in a container, while the Kubernetes Deployment config describes runtime settings, health probes, and resource limits.
tour.languageLesson: A multi-stage Dockerfile separates build-time dependencies from the production runtime image; Compose describes local services, while Kubernetes manifests describe cluster resources.

tour.title: Continuous Integration
tour.description: The CI workflow is the capstone because it exercises the same boundaries explored throughout the tour. On pushes and pull requests it runs linting, tests, and type checks, builds both backend configurations, and includes native end-to-end, container, and mobile checks.
tour.languageLesson: A GitHub Actions workflow uses events to trigger jobs and ordered steps within each job; matrix or parallel jobs can check multiple supported configurations independently.
